title: What not to put on the site for a two-sided marketplace
excerpt: Cut two equal buttons and a manifesto that comes before any match. Keep one concrete example and a way to join the side you need first. Shorter and true beats long and tasteful.
alt: A laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, beside a plant and a yellow mug, a working desk rather than a branded mood.
caption: A laptop with a code editor, a plant, and a yellow mug on a white desk. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is the first thing to remove from a marketplace homepage?
faqs.answer: Remove two equal buttons that ask the visitor to pick a side with no example behind them. Replace them with one match the scarce side would recognize and one join path in their words. The other side can have a quiet link. Equal emphasis feels fair in a meeting and empty on the page.

faqs.question: Should a marketplace site launch with a blog, a press page, and a careers page?
faqs.answer: Launch the pages that answer a job: the offer, the fee, the boundary, who is accountable, one true story, and the join path. Add a page when a real question arrives twice. Empty departments in the menu compete with the action that seeds the market.

faqs.question: How short can the site be and still be enough?
faqs.answer: Short enough that a person on a phone can find the match, the shape of the fee, and the join path without sitting through a brand film. The about page should still name an owner, and the services page should still name a refusal. Cutting filler is not a reason to become vague.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
The two-sided marketplace website mistakes that lose the scarce side are usually there to comfort the team. Cut two equal buttons and no story. Keep one concrete match and a clear way to join the side you need first. A shorter site that tells the truth will outperform a long one that performs taste.

You can feel the long version in a meeting. It looks complete. It has a manifesto, a logo row, a metric, a carousel, and a second headline for the other side. The applicant feels something else. They cannot tell what you want them to do.

## Cut the equal buttons

Two buttons of the same weight are the signature mistake. "I'm a buyer" and "I'm a seller," centered, with nothing behind them that looks like a job. The composition is fair, and it is empty. The side you need first reads it as indecision.

Replace it with one match and one action. The other side gets a text link. If a stakeholder demands both buttons, ask which side you are seeding this quarter, and style that side as the action. Fairness in the market is a result of supply. It is not a layout.

This mistake repeats in the header, the footer, and the paid landing page. Fix it everywhere or the homepage correction will be undone by the next campaign. One label, one destination, for the join path.

While you are there, cut the second slogan that tries to speak to both sides in one breath. A sentence that mentions hosts and guests in equal clauses is the equal-button problem in prose. Speak to the scarce side first. Give the other side their own sentence lower on the page, or their own page.

## Cut the manifesto that precedes the product

A founding essay above the fold reassures the people who wrote it. It confuses a person who does not know you yet and did not come for a worldview. They came to see whether a match is real and whether joining is safe enough to try.

Move any mission language below the match, the fee shape, and the boundary. If a sentence does not help someone decide to apply, it does not belong in the first two screens. Many sincere sentences fail that test. Sincerity is not a placement strategy.

Google's people-first content guidance is a clean filter here. A page should help a visitor do the thing they came to do, and it should be specific enough that it could not be pasted onto a random competitor. A manifesto about "rebuilding trust in the economy" can be pasted anywhere. A line about eight-seat dinners in one city, with the host setting the menu, cannot.

Cut the countdown, the "we're live" banner that has been up for a year, and the fake urgency around "limited spots" unless the limit is real and enforced. Manufactured pressure is a taste performance. The scarce side has a good ear for it.

## Cut proof you cannot stand behind

Logo grids of tools, accelerators, and "featured in" bars that are actually directory submissions. Vanity metrics with no denominator. Quotes you drafted and attributed to "a host." Screenshots of an empty product with fake earnings.

Keep a match you can explain: constraint, decision, outcome. Keep a number you can point to in a record. Keep a portrait of a person who agreed to be on the site and who still works the job the caption describes. Everything else is a costume, and costumes are what this buyer is trying to see through.

If you are early, a short true account beats a theatrical one. "Twelve dinners in one neighborhood, founder still confirms the menu" is a site. It does not need a timeline graphic. Publishing the theatrical version because the true one feels small is how teams end up defending copy in front of the first angry host.

Also cut the partner logos that imply an integration you do not have. A payment company mark next to your name reads as "payouts work like that company." If you simply use them as a processor, say "payouts to a bank account" and leave the logo off, unless the relationship is something a host would actually recognize as protection.

## Cut pages that exist to look like a company

A blog with no point of view, a careers page for jobs you are not hiring, a press page with no press, a "community" page that links to a silent chat. These pages are furniture. They also create navigation items that compete with Fees, Apply, and a real example.

Ship the pages that answer a job. Homepage, fees, services, about, one proof story, the join path, and a plain privacy note. Add a page when a real question arrives twice. Do not add a page because a template had a slot.

Title each page for the job. Google's guidance on title links favors titles that describe the page and that are not a repeated slogan in front of every name. "Acme | The future of local | Fees" wastes the only label a stranger sees in a list of tabs. "Fees for hosts" does the job.

Delete the stock illustrations of two abstract figures, globes, and handshakes. They are the visual form of the manifesto. The photography direction is simple: a match, or nothing. Empty space is a better neighbor for a true sentence than a picture that argues with it.

## Keep the match and the door

After the cuts, the first screen should still do three things. Show one match a peer would recognize. State the shape of the fee or point to it in the next line. Offer one join path, with what to have ready and how fast you reply.

The about page should still name who is accountable. The services page should still state a boundary. The navigation should still use their words. Cutting is not an excuse to become vague. It is how those few statements become visible.

Read the shorter site on a phone, out loud, in the time a person will actually give it. If you can say the match, the fee shape, and the next step without scrolling through a brand film, you have the site. If you miss one, put it back in words. Do not put back the carousel.

A useful test in the room: can a new teammate add a section only by removing one? If additions are free, the manifesto returns within a month, usually as a campaign. Make removal the default. The archive can hold the longer story for anyone who asks.

## How a team argues itself back into the long site

The cuts will be contested. Someone will say the page feels empty. Often they mean it feels unlike a funded company. The scarce side is not grading you on whether you look funded. They are grading you on whether the sixth seat at a table, or the next load, is real.

Someone will say both sides deserve equal billing. They do deserve a door. They do not deserve the hero on the day you are still recruiting the side that makes the door worth opening. Revisit the emphasis when that side is no longer scarce. Write down the condition, so the argument has a date instead of a vibe.

Someone will want to keep a section because it took a week to write. Sunk writing is not a reason to tax every future applicant. Thank the draft. Take the one sentence that was specific. Let the rest go.

## A pass you can run this week

Take the live homepage and circle anything that is not the match, the fee shape, or the join path. The circles are candidates, not trophies. For each one, write the reader it serves. If the only reader is the team, the investor update, or a template, remove it and look again tomorrow before you put it back.

Then open the navigation and do the same with labels. Any item you cannot connect to a job the scarce side named in the last ten applications is a candidate. Park it. A shorter menu is a product decision you can reverse, which is a better default than a long menu you will be embarrassed to explain.

Read the remaining copy for claims you could not prove in a hearing. Superlatives, "trusted by," unnamed quotes, and round numbers without a source in your own records. Replace each one with the specific fact or delete the line. The page will sound quieter. Quieter is what a skeptical host experiences as honesty.

Do not schedule a redesign to do this. The cuts can ship as copy and layout changes on the current site. A new visual system that preserves the equal buttons and the manifesto has not started the work.

The same comfort-for-the-team failure shows up when the buyer is an operator who needs to know you can move something. A globe and a container do there what equal buttons do here. That page is [what the homepage has to prove for a logistics company](/blog/what-the-homepage-has-to-prove-for-a-logistics-company).

If you want help deciding what the shorter site keeps, start with [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services).
